quests.instruction: A child has an empty glass jar. Which is a good way to reuse it?
quests.correctAnswer: Use it as a pencil holder ✏️
options: Use it as a pencil holder ✏️
quests.hint: Think of a use that keeps it out of the trash.
quests.explanation: Reusing things keeps them out of landfills and saves the resources needed to make new ones.
quests.funFact: Glass can be recycled again and again without losing quality.

quests.instruction: Which of these can go into a compost pile?
quests.hint: Think of things that were once alive and will rot.
quests.explanation: Fruit and vegetable scraps break down into rich compost that feeds plants. Plastic and batteries do not rot and can harm soil.
quests.funFact: Worms and fungi do most of the work inside a compost pile.

quests.instruction: Why does recycling aluminum cans help nature?
quests.hint: New metal takes a lot of resources to make.
quests.explanation: Making cans from recycled aluminum uses far less energy than making them from raw ore and reduces mining.
quests.funFact: Recycled aluminum can use about 95% less energy than new aluminum.

quests.instruction: A town wants to build on a pond where frogs live. Which plan protects the frogs best?
options: Move all frogs in a bucket 🪣
quests.hint: Think about keeping their home.
quests.explanation: Building on land that is already developed avoids destroying habitat. Moving animals rarely solves the problem, because they need the right home.
quests.funFact: Frogs often return to the same pond year after year.

quests.instruction: Why are national parks and nature reserves set up?
quests.hint: They are set aside for nature.
quests.explanation: Protected areas keep habitats safe so animals and plants can live and breed, and so people can enjoy nature.
quests.funFact: Some animals, like tigers and pandas, depend on protected areas to survive.

quests.instruction: A school plans a wildlife garden. Which flowers are the best choice?
quests.hint: Local insects and birds know them well.
quests.explanation: Native plants provide food and shelter for local wildlife. Invasive plants can spread and push natives out.
quests.funFact: A single native oak tree can support hundreds of kinds of insects.

quests.instruction: Many people feed bread to ducks at ponds. Why isn't this good for ducks?
options: It gives them too much energy ⚡
quests.hint: Think about what food the ducks naturally eat.
quests.explanation: Bread doesn't give ducks the nutrition they need and uneaten bits foul the water and attract pests.
quests.funFact: Wild ducks do best eating plants, insects, and seeds.

quests.instruction: A sign in the park says 'Please do not pick wildflowers.' Why?
quests.hint: Picked flowers can't finish their life cycle.
quests.explanation: If flowers are picked, plants can't make seeds, and fewer will grow next year. Insects also lose nectar.
quests.funFact: One wildflower can produce many seeds for next year.

quests.instruction: A seal pup is resting alone on a beach. What should you do?
quests.correctAnswer: Stay far away and tell an adult 🦭
options: Stay far away and tell an adult 🦭
Push it back into the sea 🌊
quests.hint: Its mother is probably nearby.
quests.explanation: Mother seals leave pups on the beach while they hunt. Humans nearby can scare the mother away and harm the pup.
quests.funFact: Seal pups often rest on shore while their mothers feed at sea.

quests.instruction: A child plants a tree seedling. Which step helps it most in its first dry summer?
options: Pull it up to check roots ✋
quests.hint: Young roots can't reach deep water yet.
quests.explanation: New trees have small root systems, so regular watering through the first summers helps them survive.
quests.funFact: A tree's roots usually spread wider than its branches.

quests.instruction: Why plant different kinds of flowers in a school garden?
quests.hint: Think about who visits a garden besides people.
quests.explanation: A mix of flowers that bloom at different times gives pollinators food from spring to autumn.
quests.funFact: Some bees only visit flowers of certain shapes.

quests.instruction: A seedling that needs full sun is planted in deep shade. What is most likely to happen?
quests.hint: Think about the plant's need for light.
quests.explanation: With too little light, plants stretch toward it and grow weak and spindly, so they need a better spot.
quests.funFact: Gardeners say 'right plant, right place'.

quests.instruction: Smoke from vehicles and factories can make the air dirty. Which choice helps?
quests.hint: Fewer engines mean fewer fumes.
quests.explanation: Walking, cycling, and public transport produce much less pollution than many separate cars.
quests.funFact: Cleaner air also helps plants and animals, not just people.

quests.instruction: Bright lights at night can confuse some animals. Which of these is often affected?
quests.hint: They use the night sky to find their way.
quests.explanation: Bright lights can attract and disorient birds flying at night. Turning off unnecessary lights helps them.
quests.funFact: Millions of birds migrate at night.

quests.instruction: Noise from ships can disturb whales. Why is that a problem?
quests.correctAnswer: They use sound to find food 🐋
options: They use sound to find food 🐋
quests.hint: Think about how whales find each other in the dark deep sea.
quests.explanation: Whales and dolphins use sounds to communicate and navigate, so loud noise can make this difficult.
quests.funFact: Blue whale calls can travel hundreds of kilometers underwater.

quests.instruction: Which action saves electricity at home?
quests.correctAnswer: Turn off lights you aren't using 💡
options: Turn off lights you aren't using 💡
quests.hint: Don't pay for light nobody uses.
quests.explanation: Making electricity often burns fuel. Using less saves resources and reduces pollution.
quests.funFact: Switching to LED bulbs can cut lighting energy a lot.

quests.instruction: Burning coal, oil, and gas adds extra carbon dioxide to the air. What can this do?
quests.hint: Some gases act like a blanket around Earth.
quests.explanation: Carbon dioxide traps heat. Adding more of it makes Earth warmer over time and can change weather and climate.
quests.funFact: Plants take in some carbon dioxide, so forests help.

quests.instruction: Which energy source can keep working without running out?
quests.hint: The wind blows again tomorrow.
quests.explanation: Wind, sunlight, and flowing water are renewable because they are replaced naturally.
quests.funFact: Wind turbines can turn steady breezes into electricity.

quests.instruction: Farmers plant different crops in the same field in different years. How does this help the soil?
quests.hint: Different plants use and return different nutrients.
quests.explanation: Rotating crops prevents the soil from being drained of the same nutrients and can reduce pests.
quests.funFact: Beans and peas add nitrogen to the soil.

quests.instruction: Why can eating foods grown nearby and in season be good for nature?
quests.hint: Think about how far food has to move.
quests.explanation: Food that travels shorter distances needs less fuel for transport, and seasonal crops often need less artificial heat or storage.
quests.funFact: Some vegetables travel thousands of kilometers to reach stores.

quests.instruction: Why is wasting less food good for the environment?
quests.hint: Growing food uses a lot.
quests.explanation: All food needs land, water, and energy to grow. Wasting less means fewer resources are used.
quests.funFact: Roughly a third of food produced is wasted.

quests.instruction: A child wants to help birds in her yard. Which choice is best?
quests.hint: Think about food, water, and safety.
quests.explanation: Native plants provide seeds and insects, and clean water helps birds drink and bathe. Chemicals and cats can harm them.
quests.funFact: A shallow dish of water can attract many birds.

quests.instruction: A 'bee hotel' made of hollow stems gives shelter to which bees?
quests.hint: Not all bees live in big hives.
quests.explanation: Many bees live alone and lay eggs in hollow stems or holes. Bee hotels give them safe spots.
quests.funFact: Most bee species in the world are solitary.

quests.instruction: Why leave a small pile of logs and leaves in a corner of the garden?
quests.hint: Think about what a quiet corner could offer an animal.
quests.explanation: Beetles, toads, and hedgehogs can use the pile for shelter and food, and it slowly turns into soil.
quests.funFact: A rotting log can host hundreds of small species.

quests.instruction: You find broken glass and a bottle on a beach. What is the safest way to help?
quests.hint: Sharp things can cut you.
quests.explanation: Broken glass is dangerous. An adult can pick it up with gloves and put it in the right bin.
quests.funFact: Beach clean-ups collect millions of pieces of litter each year.

quests.instruction: A friend wants to catch a wild frog to keep at home. What is a better choice?
options: Keep it in a jar for fun 🫙
Take it home as a pet 🏠
quests.hint: Frogs need their own habitat.
quests.explanation: Wild animals have particular needs for food, water, and shelter, and taking them can harm them and the ecosystem.
quests.funFact: Frogs help control insects when left in their habitat.

quests.instruction: Why is it a good idea to stay on marked trails when hiking?
quests.hint: Think about what repeated stepping does to the ground.
quests.explanation: Trampling plants can kill them and cause erosion, so trails guide us along tough paths.
quests.funFact: Plants on some mountain slopes take years to recover from a few footsteps.

quests.instruction: A class wants to use less paper. Which choice helps most?
quests.correctAnswer: Use both sides of each page 📄
options: Use bigger sheets for each task 📏
Use both sides of each page 📄
quests.hint: Think about getting more use from each sheet.
quests.explanation: Using both sides cuts paper use in half, which means fewer trees cut and less energy and water used to make paper.
quests.funFact: Making a single sheet of paper takes several liters of water.

quests.instruction: A class finds litter beside a stream. What should happen first?
quests.hint: Plan for safety before you start.
quests.explanation: Safe clean-ups need adult supervision and gloves, and rubbish should be sorted for the correct bins.
quests.funFact: Never touch syringes, broken glass, or unknown liquids.

quests.instruction: Why is 'take only pictures, leave only footprints' a good rule outdoors?
quests.hint: Think about what others will see after you leave.
quests.explanation: Leaving nature as you found it keeps habitats healthy so other people and wildlife can enjoy them.
quests.funFact: Many parks use the 'leave no trace' principles.
